sentences.text: Scientists have found multiple complete skeletons of Helodus simplex, revealing an internal skeleton made of cartilage instead of bone.
The first dorsal fin possessed a short, smooth spine supported by the synarcual, a specialized structure at the base of the skull, and this spine was made of osteodentin, a tooth-like tissue.
Naturalist Louis Agassiz named the genus Helodus in 1838 based on isolated bead-like teeth from the late Paleozoic.
James William Davis described a fossil skeleton of Helodus simplex in 1890, which was found in an ironstone mine in Staffordshire, England, and is now housed at the Hunterian Museum and Art Gallery.
Helodus is the sole member of the family Helodontidae and the order Helodontiformes.
Helodus belongs to the class Chondrichthyes and the subclass Holocephali, which includes living chimaeras.
Helodus simplex lived in a shallow freshwater environment.
Over 70 species have been attributed to Helodus based on similar teeth, but these likely belong to many different unrelated fish groups, making the genus a 'wastebasket taxon'.
Researchers have tentatively suggested a relationship between Helodus and the order Eugeneodontiformes based on tooth similarities, but this requires further confirmation.
